items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] El Niño winter forecast: See a map that shows which U.S. regions will get the most snow and rain
items.content_html:
This year’s Super El Niño “looms large” over the winter forecast for the United States, forecasters from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) wrote this week.

And for about half of the country, that’s shaping up to make for a wet winter. 

El Niño is a climate phenomenon defined by above-average sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, and a weakening of trade winds that flow from east to west. All those changes affect atmospheric conditions, disrupting global weather patterns.

How will the phenomenon impact U.S. weather patterns?

El Niños typically present with wetter conditions across the U.S. South, and drier than conditions farther north.

A 2026-2027 Winter Outlook map from NOAA illustrates that, showing a wavy band cutting across the U.S. that will bring “above normal” precipitation to the southern half of the country. That band swings up to cover the entire California coast and the East Coast, as well.  

Certain areas will be impacted even more: parts of Florida, for example, are forecasted to experience 70-80% above normal precipitation.

“As we know from decades of observations, a very strong El Niño will likely bring a southward and eastward shift to the jet stream for the contiguous U.S., which tilts the odds toward stormier weather across the South,” Ken Graham, director of NOAA’s National Weather Service (NWS), said in a statement. 

That wet weather could ease drought conditions in the southwest. Southern Great Plains, Southeast, and parts of the East Coast, according to another NOAA map. 

But forecasters say that could make for other negative weather impacts.

“While higher chances of rain and snow may bring relief to drought-afflicted areas, too much precipitation on dry soil can fuel destructive flash floods and mudslides,” Graham said. “Now is the time for communities and individuals to plan ahead for the upcoming winter.” 

Some communities are already preparing. Governor Gavin Newsom of California has already declared a state of emergency ahead of this El Niño winter. 

With this El Niño already breaking records and potentially only getting stronger, “that can mean repeated rounds of heavy rain, strong winds, mountain snow, flooding, landslides, debris flows, large waves, and coastal flooding, especially when storms hit during very high tides” for California, according to his office. 

Certain areas of the country are expected to see drier-than-average conditions, though, like Hawaii, Alaska, the northern Mountain West, and some areas around the Great Lakes.

That also means drought conditions could “develop or worsen,” forecasters wrote, across some of the northern Rockies, as well as northeastern Oregon and eastern Washington.

Those forecasts mirror others looking ahead to this winter, including a series of maps from AccuWeather that was shared with Fast Company earlier this month.

Word to the wise: The map is not the territory

Experts do note that specific outcomes aren’t a guarantee; the El Niño simply tilts the odds toward certain impacts. As the season gets closer, meteorologists will continue to update their forecasts. 

For those who want to keep a close eye on any oncoming snow or rain, the NWS has now opened its Probabilistic Precipitation Portal, an interactive map that lets users see “the low-end, expected, and high-end amounts of snow, ice and rain” over a 72-hour period.

items.title: [ArchDaily] World Monuments Watch 2027 Nominations Point to Government Austerity, Climate Impact and Skills Shortages as Main Threats to Heritage
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The World Monuments Fund (WMF), an independent nonprofit organization dedicated to the preservation of historic architecture and cultural heritage since 1965, receives nominations through the World Monuments Watch, a flagship advocacy and conservation program. Every two years, the Watch selects 25 sites from the nominations received from individuals and community-based organizations worldwide. Nominations for the 2027 World Monuments Watch closed on March 20, 2026, with a total of 372 public nominations from 84 countries and territories. Before announcing the selected sites in early 2027, the WMF offers an analysis of the nominations. Global data shows three main causes of heritage endangerment worldwide: government austerity, intensifying climate impact, and lack of access to specialized skills and expertise. At a time when political priorities tend to stray from history, the call is to recognize heritage sites as an area of shared opportunity rather than a burden.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Half of the world’s population has been exposed to heat waves and wildfire smoke at the same time
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Climate change is a global phenomenon, meaning that everyone, in some way, will feel its devastating impacts. 

And increasingly, those impacts are happening simultaneously: Over the past two decades, more than half of the world’s population has experienced simultaneous heat waves and wildfires, occurring on the same day, a study found.

Researchers at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, published their findings this week in the journal Science Advances.

The study looked at 20 years of data, from 2000 to 2019. To see who experienced a wildfire, researchers looked at who was exposed to “fire-sourced air pollution”; their data took into account hourly temperature, fire emissions, air quality, and population information.

Over those 20 years, researchers found, the number of people around the world exposed to both wildfires and heat waves, on the same days, increased by 287 million—from 761 million people per year in the first half of that time period to more than 1 billion people per year in the second.

That means 55.9% of the global population has experienced at least one day where a heat wave and wildfire pollution occurred in tandem.

And the number of such days is increasing. From 2000 to 2009, the average person experienced one such day per year. Between 2010 and 2019, that rose to 1.7 days of co-exposure per person.

Damaging on multiple levels

The research doesn’t only illustrate how climate change is making extreme weather more frequent. It also shows how the health impacts of these events can compound as extreme weather overlaps.

Both heat waves and wildfires can cause serious harm to our health. Along with the risk of heatstroke—which can damage your brain, heart, and kidneys, and even be fatal—extreme heat and humidity can make it harder for some people to breathe, especially those with asthma or other lung conditions. 

Wildfires come with intense air pollution, full of tiny particles called PM2.5 (particulate matter 2.5 micrometers or less in diameter) that can get into our lungs and bloodstream, raising the risk of heart attack, stroke, and reduced lung function.

When heat waves combine with air pollution, the health impacts exacerbate. On days when an area sees a “double whammy” of high heat and high air pollution, the risk of death is three times greater “than the effect of either high heat or high air pollution alone,” health researchers have previously written. 

The Monash University researchers emphasize this in their study, too. “Compared with exposure to heat wave or landscape fire-sourced air pollution alone, co-exposure to both hazards may exert greater health impacts than the sum of their individual effects,” they write. 

In other words, the health risks—including respiratory and cardiovascular impacts—become amplified when wildfire air pollution and extreme heat happen together.

Extreme heat and wildfires also impact each event occurring. Conditions like high temperatures and dry soil promote wildfires, and wildfires then exacerbate heat waves because they release heat and pollution into the air.

“These processes create a positive feedback loop in which heat waves and fires amplify one another,” the researchers wrote.

Which regions are being hit hardest?

Some regions of the world are experiencing these simultaneous effects more than others. Zambia, for example, sees more than 28 such days per person every year. The Democratic Republic of the Congo comes in second, with just over 24 days per person per year.

Countries with lower life expectancy, education, and income tended to see the highest amount of wildfire and heat co-exposure, an example of the way that climate change is hitting the world’s poorest countries the hardest. 

Still, almost every area of the world saw an increase in this trend.

Central America, South America, Central and Eastern Africa, Southeast Asia, and parts of North America, Australia, and Russia all experienced “notable increases” in the annual average number of days that wildfire pollution and extreme heat occurred together.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] The hidden costs of fracking: boom in Argentina linked to trail of sickness
items.content_html:
Families in Vaca Muerta, the centre of Patagonia’s shale operation, report cancers, miscarriages and pollution

In Allen, a small town in Argentine Patagonia, many people living on the same street ended up falling ill. For some, it was severe migraines, nausea or skin irritation. For others, cancers, congenital abnormalities, miscarriages or stillbirth seemed to affect foetuses or children. People say it all started 13 years ago – when a well was drilled near their homes to extract gas and oil.

Calle Ciega 10 [Dead-end Street 10] lies on the eastern edge of Vaca Muerta, a vital area for Argentina’s economy, home to the world’s second-largest reserve of shale gas and fourth-largest reserve of shale oil. The region has more than 2,600 active wells, including one on this small street where about 20 families live, most of them seasonal workers on fruit farms.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘I am still a child, it cannot be good to be married’: how drought forces Afghan families to sell girls as brides
items.content_html:
As climate breakdown pushes families to starvation, many feel forced to ‘sacrifice’ daughters to save siblings. Photographer Elise Blanchard travelled the country speaking to girls as young as eight, 10 and 14 who have been engaged or married to repay debts or pay for food

‘I’m not happy about this,” says 11-year-old Khatira, who was sold into marriage to repay debts, sitting in her home in Qala-e-Naw, capital of Badghis province in north-west Afghanistan. “She was healthy before her engagement, now she is worried and cries a lot,” says her 40-year-old mother, Noor Bibi.

When her 20-year-old husband-to-be comes to her home, Khatira runs away. Since her engagement, she has stopped going outside because she “is ashamed of having a husband in front of the other girls”, says her mother.

Shepherds watch over their sheep in the hills of Bala-Murghab, Badghis province, north-west Afghanistan. By March, the pasture was already too dry for the season
